headline: Several of today's papers find that the measuring tools themselves are wrong: benchmark success checkers, physics scores, world-model costs and age or persona prompts report things that are not true. The useful fixes diagnose where the failure is before anyone retrains a model.
thesis: Today's papers share one move: they stop trusting the number and check what produced it. Success checkers in RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa365 and RoboDojo accept unfinished executions and reject valid ones. Physics-IQ rewards video models for blurring. A world-model planner's cost can be at chance on predicted outcomes while it is sound on real ones. VLMs told to answer as an older adult move valence in the direction opposite to what older people actually report. The same diagnostic habit shows up at runtime. Planners break stalls instead of adapting weights, large reasoning models are called only when a monitor flags trouble, and safety work measures what the robot physically does after it stops, not only whether the task was completed. For a team building robots for people of many ages and cultures, the most direct lesson is that human-likeness has to be checked against measured human data, item by item, and a demographic prompt does not provide that.

clusters.title: The evaluators are now being audited, and success checkers, physics scores and episode-level success rates all overstate progress
clusters.why: Benchmark numbers have usually been taken at face value once a checker accepts an expert demonstration. SimAudit finds 61 checker defects across 49 tasks, 40 of which accept incomplete executions. Kernel Physics-IQ shows that the official physics score can go up while predicted futures collapse. Mind2Act shows that a system that passes reasoning-only and execution-only tasks drops to 12.0% when the two must be combined, and AgentRoboCritic moves analysis from episodes to individual actions. AFFECT raises the correlation between world-model and real-robot policy success on DROID from 0.47 to 0.79, which is the property that decides whether a world model can stand in for real evaluation. Before you trust a sim benchmark or a world-model evaluator for go/no-go decisions, test its checker on partial and alternative executions and correlate it with real rollouts.

clusters.title: World-model planners mostly fail in the planning loop (stalls, search, scoring), so diagnose the failure type before retraining the model
clusters.why: The usual explanation for a failing world-model planner is model error under distribution shift, and the usual fix is test-time weight adaptation. Stuck in Place finds that at least 96% of JEPA planner failures on pushing tasks are stalls at a fixed point of the planning loop, which random re-initialization or a residual error memory can break without new weights. Search or Scoring separates the two failure types and finds that on Metaworld the cost is sound on real outcomes (AUROC 0.94) but at chance on predictions (0.54), so a larger search does not help there. Verify2Act, Fast-JEPA and GEMS each add structure around a frozen world model (a critic, direct prediction of complete candidates, generated subgoals plus memory) instead of a better model. If your world-model planner underperforms, log whether it is stalling, missing good candidates, or mis-ranking them, because each needs a different fix.

clusters.title: Large reasoning models are being moved off the control loop and called on events, with little or no loss in success
clusters.why: Agentic and VLA stacks often query the large model at every step or chunk, which costs latency and tokens on robots. RoC calls its reasoning agent only when an online task-state monitor flags trouble and reports 24.0 points more success with 65.3% fewer tokens than the strongest agent-based baseline. CHAC cuts navigation VLM calls by 33.4% to 64.7%, although success drops by 10.82 points on R2R-CE. FastRoverVLA reuses decoded off-road plans with motion correction at request rates near 5%. R2-VLA asks a human expert only when calibrated uncertainty exceeds a threshold set by a target failure risk, and CauSyncVLA overlaps inference with execution at 5.04x throughput. For deployed robots, treat model calls as a budget: put a cheap monitor or uncertainty gate in front of the expensive model and measure success per call.

clusters.title: Modelling people of different ages and preferences takes measured human signals, not demographic prompts
clusters.why: A common shortcut for personalising robot or agent behaviour is to put the user's age or persona in the prompt. Across 17 VLMs and 822 human raters, an older-adult prompt lowers rated valence on pleasant images by 0.845 points while older participants actually rate them 0.443 points higher, and model-human age effects barely correlate (at most 0.093). Persona Lenses finds that the most separating prompt is also the least robust to irrelevant profile changes. The constructive papers measure people directly: HumanCOIN records gaze, EMG and EEG as intent traces, a role-allocation framework reads hand-object entropy and spoken preferences while leaving the human free to take initiative, and an exoskeleton controller is trained on a simulated human and then tested on five unseen people. If your robot adapts to age or culture, validate that adaptation against per-stimulus human data from those groups before shipping it.

clusters.title: Touch and physical properties help a policy only where they carry information that vision cannot predict
clusters.why: This continues yesterday's finding that touch helps when it is gated rather than fused raw. TacInno reports that much of the tactile change in visuo-tactile VLAs is predictable from vision and executed actions, so it trains only on the unpredictable part (tactile innovation) and adds no module at deployment. TipDex-VTLA trusts touch more when visual action reliability drops under lighting changes, reaching 73.8% under unseen challenging lighting. PhyDEX shows the cost of lacking physical information: three VLAs score below 3% on throwing tasks, and giving them ground-truth mass, center of mass and friction roughly doubles success. When you add a sensor or a physics estimate to a policy, measure what it adds beyond what the camera already implies.

clusters.title: Silent failures are the deployment risk, and several papers add explicit checks on what the robot does when it should not be trusted
clusters.why: Safety and robustness are often scored as task non-completion or average error. SAFI shows that a VLA trained to refuse a task from its initial state can still complete it when taking over mid-execution, or drop the object it is holding, and teaches a holding response that cuts takeover completion to 1.3% with no recorded physical incidents. DMT-Attack shows that natural-looking tablecloth textures disrupt pi0.5 and OpenVLA-OFT while evading a detector far more often than patch attacks. Conformal pose sets calibrated on synthetic images fail silently on up to 43.5% of real images, and multi-robot LiDAR registration adds plausibility checks that reject more than a third of wrong alignments. Passage-conditioned navigation stores how each ledge was entered so the robot backs up and retries instead of falling. Add a check for 'am I in a state where my output is wrong without knowing it', and evaluate stopping behaviour mid-task, not only from the start state.

insights: Audit your benchmark before you trust its leaderboard. SimAudit finds both phantom successes and silent failures in three widely used simulated manipulation suites, and Kernel Physics-IQ shows a physics metric that rewards collapsed predictions. If your team reports sim success to decide what goes on the robot, feed each checker a few deliberately partial executions and a few valid but unusual ones, and treat any checker that misjudges them as a bug in your evaluation, not noise.

Age and culture adaptation cannot be prompted into a model and assumed correct. The age-conditioned affect study is the clearest result today for a team building robots for people of different ages: the models shift in the direction a stereotype predicts, while real older adults shift the other way on the very images where it matters. Any persona-conditioned behaviour (tone, emotional reading, content filtering) should be scored against stimulus-level ratings from the target group, and the persona-lens results suggest checking it is unaffected by profile attributes that should not matter.

Before retraining, find out where the loop breaks. Stall diagnosis, search-versus-scoring diagnosis, RoC's event-triggered agent review and Mind2Act's failure attribution all decide where the failure sits before anything is retrained. Logging that separates 'the plan stalled', 'the candidate was never tried', 'the cost ranked it wrong' and 'reasoning and execution did not compose' is cheap to add and tells you whether to spend compute on search, on the model, or on the interface between planner and policy.

Measure stopping and refusal behaviour from mid-task states, with the physical outcome recorded. SAFI's finding that refusal from the initial state does not transfer to takeover partway through matters for any robot handing objects to people: a drop is a safety incident even if the forbidden task was not completed. Add mid-execution interruption tests with a held object to your safety evaluation.

must_read.why: The most direct evidence today on whether foundation models can stand in for how people of different ages perceive emotional content, which is core to robots meant to interact across age groups.
must_read.key_idea: Compare a model's change under an age prompt with the actual age differences in human ratings of the same image, rather than checking only whether the model reacts to the prompt.
must_read.evidence: 17 VLMs, 900 OASIS images, ratings from 822 participants. Without an age cue, models track average valence (median r = 0.891), but correlations between model and human age effects range from -0.030 to 0.093 against a ceiling of 0.595. On 54 sensitive pleasant images, the older-adult prompt lowers valence by 0.845 points while older participants rate them 0.443 points higher.
must_read.caveat: It covers static image valence ratings in three age bands, not interaction, speech or culture, and the abstract does not say which cultures or countries the participants came from.

must_read.why: If your team picks policies or checkpoints on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa365 or RoboDojo, some of those success numbers are wrong in a known direction.
must_read.key_idea: Use an LLM to read the instruction and the checker code, predict scenarios where they disagree, recreate them in simulation and verify the outcome visually.
must_read.evidence: 183 simulated test cases produced the predicted checker verdict, and visual verification and deduplication left 61 distinct defects across 49 tasks (40 phantom successes, 21 silent failures). RoboCasa365 errs mostly toward accepting incomplete runs, RoboDojo mostly toward rejecting valid ones.
must_read.caveat: The abstract does not quantify how much these defects change reported policy rankings, and the auditor's own coverage (defects it misses) is not estimated.

must_read.why: It gives a cheap, concrete diagnostic for any team using DINO-WM or JEPA-style world models for planning, and tells you whether more search or a better model will help.
must_read.key_idea: Separate search failures (a good action was never tried) from scoring failures (the cost on predicted outcomes ranks a bad action first) by executing candidates and comparing costs on predicted and real outcomes.
must_read.evidence: On Metaworld the cost scores real outcomes well (AUROC 0.94) but predicted outcomes at chance (0.54). Averaging retrieved demonstration windows without the model solves 127 of 168 new Metaworld tasks against at most 87 when the model chooses, and a pre-registered rule solves 678 of 960 PushT episodes against 530 for the best fixed strategy.
must_read.caveat: Simulation only, on short tasks whose goals the planner can represent; it is not shown whether the diagnosis holds on long-horizon or real-robot tasks.

must_read.why: It changes how to evaluate a VLA's refusal: for a robot working near people, what happens to the object in the gripper after a stop matters as much as whether the task stopped.
must_read.key_idea: Train an explicit fallback (stationary arm, consistent gripper) at intermediate states of prohibited-task demonstrations, alongside the retained tasks.
must_read.evidence: Policies that suppress a task from its initial state can still complete it when taking over partway, and may drop held objects. With OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO and BadLIBERO, SAFI reduces target success after takeover to 1.3% with no recorded physical incidents or action saturation, while retained-task success stays high.
must_read.caveat: Simulation only, a single VLA backbone, and the method assumes that holding is an appropriate fallback, which may not hold when a person is pulling the object or the robot is mid-handover.

must_read.why: The day's one dedicated HRI paper, and it lets the human take initiative instead of being assigned tasks, which matters for acceptance by users who want to stay in charge.
must_read.key_idea: Leave the human free to act, and allocate the robot's activities dynamically through a cost-driven behaviour tree that reads spoken preferences via an LLM and monitors hand-object interaction with Shannon entropy.
must_read.evidence: A pilot study and a 14-participant experiment indicate intuitive, engaging collaboration without higher perceived workload; the framework also detects anomalies in human execution and triggers corrective robot actions.
must_read.caveat: The abstract gives no numerical effect sizes or comparison condition, and 14 participants on one task leaves open how it behaves across ages, cultures or ambiguous instructions.

2611.25179.problem: Simulated manipulation benchmarks rely on hand-written success checkers that are validated only against expert demonstrations.
2611.25179.method: SimAudit uses an LLM to find instruction-checker disagreements, recreates them in sim, and verifies outcomes from multi-view renderings.
2611.25179.why: It finds 61 defects across 49 tasks in RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa365 and RoboDojo, so sim success numbers used for model selection can be wrong in either direction.

2611.25632.problem: Physics-IQ compares a generated video with one recording, so it can reward blurred or collapsed predictions when several futures are valid.
2611.25632.method: Kernel Physics-IQ removes this incentive in expectation using two independent samples per condition.
2611.25632.why: If you rank video world models by physics scores, fewer denoising steps can look better while being worse, and this metric catches it.

2611.26444.problem: Benchmarks test reasoning and execution separately or mixed, so they cannot tell which one causes a failure.
2611.26444.method: Mind2Act World splits 30 sim tasks into memory-based decisions, precise execution, and closed-loop tasks that need both, with a harness that attributes failures.
2611.26444.why: The strongest agent drops from 52.7% (Mind) and 39.0% (Act) to 12.0% when both are needed, which points to the planner-policy interface as the place to invest.

2611.26613.problem: Episode success rates hide how frontier agents that output low-level robot actions succeed or fail.
2611.26613.method: The agent states a local intent with each action, and a critic judges the outcome and failure mode against that intent; a fine-tuned open critic is released.
2611.26613.why: Action-level failure labels (grasping and alignment are the bottleneck) are more useful for debugging than success rates, and the critic's failure-mode accuracy rises from 32.58% to 74.24%.

2611.25980.problem: Video world models look realistic but respond poorly to small action changes, which limits them for policy evaluation.
2611.25980.method: AFFECT injects correlated noise into actions and trains the model so its videos respond to it as recorded videos do.
2611.25980.why: On DROID the correlation between world-model and real-robot policy success rises from 0.47 to 0.79, which is the property that matters if you want to evaluate policies offline.

2611.25415.problem: JEPA planners fail on tasks their model should handle, and test-time adaptation assumes model error is the cause.
2611.25415.method: Tracing the planning loop shows most failures are stalls at a fixed point; Unstick breaks them with an error memory or random re-initialization at replan.
2611.25415.why: At least 96% of failures were stalls, so a fixed-weight loop breaker can recover much of the gain usually attributed to adaptation.

2611.25347.problem: When a visual world-model planner fails, it does not record whether the search or the cost was to blame.
2611.25347.method: Execute the optimizer's candidates and compare costs on predicted versus real outcomes, then choose between warm-starting from demonstrations and model-free averaging.
2611.25347.why: It tells you whether to buy more search or a better model; on Metaworld the predicted-outcome cost is at chance even though the real-outcome cost is sound.

2611.25243.problem: VLM-proposed manipulation plans are not grounded in how the scene will change, and pixel world models are slow and drift.
2611.25243.method: A latent world model in DINOv2 space imagines each candidate plan and a dual-head critic checks it before execution; training uses only digital-twin data.
2611.25243.why: On a low-cost arm it reaches 83.3% against 53.3% for the VLM alone, and all remaining failures were low-level grasp or placement slips rather than planning errors.

2611.25927.problem: Comparing candidate plans in a latent world model through recursive rollout is slow at test time.
2611.25927.method: Fast-JEPA builds a goal-directed plan and predicts outcomes of complete candidates directly, avoiding recursive rollouts; it adds the DynaGoal benchmark for deadlines and delays.
2611.25927.why: It reports 96.50% average success with 2.41x faster planning than INTACT, and it tests behaviour under execution deadlines, which most planning benchmarks skip.

2611.25134.problem: Long-horizon world-model planning suffers from compounding prediction error and weak distant-goal similarity.
2611.25134.method: GEMS combines generated subgoals with states retrieved from experience memory, with a distance gate choosing which to score against.
2611.25134.why: Using generated and remembered subgoals together around a frozen world model gains 7.3 to 24.0 points over the strongest baseline in sim.

2611.26341.problem: Calling a large multimodal model often during long-horizon manipulation costs latency and tokens.
2611.26341.method: An online task-state monitor tracks subtask progress and triggers agent review only for execution repair or plan revision.
2611.26341.why: It reports 24.0 points more success with 65.3% fewer tokens than the strongest agent baseline, plus three real long-horizon tasks.

2611.25587.problem: VLM-based navigation policies re-infer too often for onboard compute.
2611.25587.method: CHAC, which needs no training, decides how many cached waypoints to execute before re-querying, based on visual context, completion cues and controller feedback.
2611.25587.why: On real robots it cut model calls by 54.9% and GPU time by 49.7% with 18 versus 14 successes in 40 runs, though R2R-CE success fell by 10.82 points.

2611.26242.problem: Off-road VLA planners are expensive to call every update, and reused plans drift as the vehicle moves.
2611.26242.method: A speed-curvature action buffer is corrected against measured motion between visual predictions, with a reuse budget set by how rough the plan is.
2611.26242.why: It works with any backbone and needs no training; request cost drops 16.6x to 20.8x while FDE improves, which is a template for any mobile base running a slow VLA.

2611.26438.problem: Retrieval-augmented VLAs can fail even with relevant demonstrations, and there is no guarantee on how often.
2611.26438.method: R2-VLA learns action uncertainty given the retrieved context and calibrates a threshold so that task failure risk meets a user target, asking an expert otherwise.
2611.26438.why: It turns 'when should the robot ask for help' into a calibrated setting, with 9.2 to 11.2 points more success and fewer expert requests on LIBERO.

2611.25667.problem: Overlapping VLA inference with execution leaves perceptual memory stale and action chunks disconnected.
2611.25667.method: A causal latent world model predicts current perceptual memory from delayed frames and executed actions, and warm-starts flow correction of the unexecuted horizon.
2611.25667.why: Asynchronous control at 5.04x throughput with 93.8% on LIBERO-10 matters for smooth motion on real arms, though only sim results are reported.

2611.25593.problem: Age-prompted VLMs are used to simulate how different people perceive images, without checking against those people.
2611.25593.method: Compare per-image model age effects for 17 VLMs with age differences estimated from 822 human raters on 900 OASIS images.
2611.25593.why: The models shift in the opposite direction from real older adults on pleasant sensitive images, so age-personalised robot behaviour needs stimulus-level human validation.

2611.25508.problem: A persona in the prompt only partly changes where a VLM predicts a user will look.
2611.25508.method: It compares a text lens, a pixel lens and a trained weight lens for making simulated gaze differ between personas that differ in one attribute.
2611.25508.why: The most separating method is the least robust to irrelevant profile changes, which is a useful warning for any user-model in an interactive robot.

2611.26434.problem: Egocentric manipulation datasets record observation-action pairs but not the intent behind actions.
2611.26434.method: HumanCOIN records 12,500 hours with tiered intent proxies: inferred gaze (10,000 h), surface EMG (2,000 h) and EEG (500 h), plus depth, poses and step annotations.
2611.26434.why: Gaze and muscle-load signals that precede the hand are the cues a collaborative robot needs to anticipate a person, and this is a large source to train on.

2611.26090.problem: Role allocation in human-robot collaboration usually assigns tasks to the human too, which limits initiative and can conflict with intent.
2611.26090.method: A cost-driven behaviour tree allocates only the robot's tasks using LLM-parsed preferences and entropy-based monitoring of hand-object interactions.
2611.26090.why: Users keep initiative and the robot fills in and corrects anomalies, without higher perceived workload in a 14-person study.

2611.25480.problem: Tuning balance-assist exoskeleton controllers requires exposing people to many destabilising perturbations.
2611.25480.method: Train an RL controller against a muscle-driven virtual human built from one subject's motion capture, then deploy it on hardware with inertial sensing only.
2611.25480.why: On five unseen people it raised withstood perturbation by 11.8%, with benefits varying by body mass and recovery strategy, which is relevant to assistive robots for older adults.

2611.26485.problem: Commercial surgical robots with force feedback are closed, which blocks open research on haptic shared control.
2611.26485.method: An open-source ROS 2 framework couples a compact 3-DOF Haply Inverse3 plus tracked grip orientation to 6-DOF dVRK commands, with two guidance modes.
2611.26485.why: It is ROS 2-native and reusable for shared-control studies, and simple linear guidance significantly reduced contacts and completion time for inexperienced users.

2611.26405.problem: Adding touch to VLAs gives inconsistent gains because much of the tactile signal is predictable from vision and actions.
2611.26405.method: Encode only the unpredictable part of future tactile change as a discrete code and use it as an auxiliary training target, with nothing extra at deployment.
2611.26405.why: It beats the strongest visuo-tactile baseline by 10.7 points in sim and 9.0 on four real tasks, and it gives you a test of whether your tactile sensor adds anything.

2611.25683.problem: Lighting changes cause action drift in dexterous manipulation even when the physical state is unchanged.
2611.25683.method: Estimate how sensitive visual actions are to illumination and use tactile forecast-versus-measured discrepancy to gate bounded corrections.
2611.25683.why: Trained under normal lighting, it keeps 73.8% success under unseen challenging lighting on real tasks, which matters for robots in homes with changing light.

2611.26565.problem: VLA benchmarks rarely test whether policies reason about mass, friction and center of mass.
2611.26565.method: PhyDEX is a throwing benchmark with 35K automatically generated trajectories across randomised physical properties.
2611.26565.why: Three current VLAs score below 3%, and providing ground-truth physics roughly doubles success, so physical blindness is a real gap.

2611.26239.problem: VLAs that refuse a prohibited task from the start can still complete it, or drop the held object, when taking over mid-execution.
2611.26239.method: SAFI builds fallback targets (hold still, keep the grip) at intermediate states and trains them jointly with retained tasks.
2611.26239.why: It cuts takeover completion to 1.3% with no recorded physical incidents, and it shows why non-completion alone is a poor safety metric.

2611.25695.problem: Adversarial patches against VLAs are conspicuous and easy to detect.
2611.25695.method: Search a diffusion model's natural-image space for tablecloth-like textures using closed-loop rollout feedback, without gradients.
2611.25695.why: Natural textures reach a 57.9% clean-conditioned attack success rate on pi0.5 and OpenVLA-OFT while evading a detector far more often than patches, which matters for robots in uncontrolled homes.

2611.26065.problem: Conformal uncertainty sets calibrated on synthetic images lose their coverage guarantee on real images.
2611.26065.method: Calibrate on synthetic images translated to real appearance, which keeps the geometric labels valid.
2611.26065.why: Silent failures fall from up to 43.5% to at most 3.3%, and the same sim-calibration trap applies to robot pose estimators.

2611.26276.problem: Single-scan multi-robot LiDAR registration can fail silently in aliased environments.
2611.26276.method: Pairwise coarse-to-fine alignment with deterministic plausibility checks that reject impossible pose hypotheses, using mutual observations.
2611.26276.why: It rejects more than a third of wrong registrations while falsely rejecting under 1% of correct ones, and releases a four-robot dataset.

2611.25788.problem: A collision-free detour can put a legged robot at a stair or ledge at an angle its fixed skill cannot handle.
2611.25788.method: Store each taught crossing from a 27-minute session and gate entry so the robot backs up and retries when more than 10 cm or 10° off.
2611.25788.why: It needs no training or robot model, raises in-tolerance crossings from 24.1% to 88.6%, and suits patrol robots that repeat a route.

2611.25105.problem: Coordinated multi-arm manipulation needs to predict teammates' actions and the future they jointly create.
2611.25105.method: MAWAM jointly denoises all robots' action chunks and future views with cross-agent attention from a single-robot world-action backbone.
2611.25105.why: Across three real tasks (bag collection, towel folding, umbrella handover) it reaches 67.8% mean success, 18.9 points above MA-VLA trained on the same data.

2611.25215.problem: Legged navigation in the wild needs both robust locomotion and semantic reasoning about signs and risk.
2611.25215.method: ROAM turns VLM-assigned semantic costs into a dense risk map that conditions RL locomotion and local navigation policies.
2611.25215.why: Kilometre-scale hikes with minimal intervention, and the authors report VLM reliability and spatial reasoning as the remaining gaps.

2611.25138.problem: Hand-written driving planners are assumed obsolete compared with learned ones.
2611.25138.method: Sixteen textbook planners replace only UniAD's planner on its frozen perception across nuScenes, nuPlan and HUGSIM.
2611.25138.why: Nine of sixteen beat the learned planner on HUGSIM, and 31 of 182 crashes were the planner's fault, which is a reminder to benchmark classical baselines on mobile bases.

2611.26420.problem: Egocentric video datasets lack synchronized whole-body motion for humanoid loco-manipulation.
2611.26420.method: Around 50,000 hours of egocentric stereo with whole-body motion supervise a shared action expert that predicts human and retargeted robot actions.
2611.26420.why: Human pretraining data follows an empirical scaling law and reaches 93.75% on eight real tasks, ahead of GR00T N1.7 and pi0.5.

2611.25801.problem: Human body estimators for retargeting are either slow or inaccurate, and rarely connect the body to the scene.
2611.25801.method: FAB predicts dense body points and contacts, fits SMPL quickly, and retargets motion to a Unitree G1.
2611.25801.why: Real-time single-person body estimation on a consumer GPU with closer G1 retargeting is useful both for imitation and for perceiving people around the robot.

2611.26596.problem: Monolithic VLAs struggle when long-horizon loco-manipulation couples timing, skills and precision.
2611.26596.method: A predicate-based state machine gates phases, VLA skills run within phases, and world-coordinate locking holds spatial consistency.
2611.26596.why: It hands timing and precision to classical components that need no training and are easy to inspect, shown on a Unitree G1 in sim and one real task.

2611.26218.problem: Cue-driven humanoid reaction generation handles few modalities and produces physically implausible motion.
2611.26218.method: A discrete-continuous mixture of transformers predicts states from text, audio or video cues, and an action transformer executes them in physics simulation.
2611.26218.why: Reacting appropriately to speech and gesture cues is core to social humanoids, though results are simulation-only.

2611.25529.problem: Generalist policies execute atomic skills but stall on long-horizon compositions, and self-collected data stays in-distribution.
2611.25529.method: A frozen VLM watches and names the next step in the policy's own instruction format; successful coached rollouts are relabeled and used for fine-tuning.
2611.25529.why: Unassisted long-horizon success rises from 47.4% to 59.3%, 9.8 points above fine-tuning on human demonstrations, with the action backbone frozen.

2611.25251.problem: RL post-training of humanoid VLAs is unsafe on hardware and exploits sim-to-real gaps in simulation.
2611.25251.method: Align an action-conditioned video world model with 20 autonomous real rollouts per task and run closed-loop RL inside it with the VLA and whole-body controller.
2611.25251.why: World-model RL raises mean success from 23.3% to 75.0% against 48.3% for real-robot RL, with no teleoperation needed.
